events.description: US-Taliban withdrawal deal signed. The hosts say the Taliban then went on the offensive and rejected a ceasefire.
Taliban issued a fatwa about seven days after the deal, saying they did not fight for democracy or power-sharing but to re-establish the Islamic Emirate with Hibatullah as emir.
After the deal, the Taliban carried out about 4,500 attacks in 45 days, according to Reuters.
ISIS-claimed attack on a funeral in Nangarhar, 'last week' relative to publication.
Attack on a maternity ward in Kabul, 'last week' relative to publication.
Taliban attack at a Kandahar provincial council meeting killed Gen. Raziq. Gen. Miller was nearly killed.
The TTP declared the Islamic Emirate of Waziristan.
Al-Qaeda in Iraq created the Islamic State of Iraq, ruling parts of Anbar, Diyala, Salahuddin and Mosul.
ISIS declared a caliphate and set up provinces to compete with al-Qaeda's proto-emirates.
French intervention in Mali (Operation Serval, per hosts) against al-Qaeda and allies building an emirate.
Obama said in 2012 that the 'time of war began in Afghanistan, and this is where it will end'.
John Brennan called the caliphate-building project in Iraq an 'absurd, feckless delusion'.
Bin Laden, Zawahiri and other al-Qaeda leaders escaped Tora Bora because the US relied on local militias and a light footprint.
US airstrikes against the Islamic Courts Union and then Shabab began, continuing for 14 years.
US-Taliban withdrawal deal signed in Doha, calling for a 5,000 for 1,000 prisoner swap.
Donald Trump campaigned accusing Obama of being the founder of ISIS for withdrawing troops from Iraq.
Qasem Soleimani killed alongside the PMF leader.

key_claims: The hosts argue that 'endless wars' is better called 'endless jihad': the wars continue because jihadists keep fighting, regardless of US presence.
Al-Qaeda and ISIS both fight to build local emirates leading to a global caliphate; ISIS's provinces were a deliberate attempt to carve out al-Qaeda's proto-emirates.

Al-Shabaab is described as the 'Taliban of Africa' and as al-Qaeda's most effective branch, closest to building an emirate outside Afghanistan; its members pledge allegiance to Zawahiri and Hibatullah Akhundzada.

Most of al-Qaeda's resources go to so-called local conflicts that are part of a global jihad, not only to attacking the West; the Islamic Caucasus Emirate is cited as an example of an affiliate wrongly dismissed as purely local.
The Taliban went on the offensive after the 29 Feb 2020 deal, rejected a ceasefire, and still seek to re-establish the Islamic Emirate under Hibatullah, with no evidence of willingness to reconcile.
The hosts say the Taliban are not a real counterterrorism partner against ISIS, and criticize Pompeo and US military leaders for whitewashing them.
The hosts say the US missed a chance to kill bin Laden, Zawahiri and Mullah Omar at Tora Bora because of Rumsfeld's light-footprint strategy.
Obama's vision of ISIS's predecessor as a local 'mafia' or 'JV team' is cited as a policy failure; Petraeus argued it had global aspirations.
The Taliban's stated goal remains re-establishing the Islamic Emirate rather than reconciling with the Afghan government.
The US-Taliban Doha deal repeated and enlarged the lopsided Bergdahl-style swap (5,000 Taliban prisoners for 1,000).
The Taliban have not been beaten in 19 years partly because of Pakistani support, and al-Qaeda remains the Taliban's longest-standing ally.
The US military 'pivot' from jihadist wars to great-power competition has largely already happened; Indo-Pacific Command has four times the personnel of any other command.
Obama's announced surge timeline undermined the Afghan mission, as Taliban commanders said they would wait the US out.
Jihadists will keep fighting regardless of US withdrawal, risking attacks on Americans and the West.
